subject: [PATCH 0/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node

reviews.author: Ackerley Tng
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Ackerley Tng noted that a similar problem was encountered where guest memory was charged to the thread's parent mm->owner, and suggested using a workaround involving a separate process to set the child process's memcg to the desired one, which could potentially work for NUMA allocations.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng questioned the scope and feasibility of implementing per-file memory policies for guest_memfd, suggesting that a default filesystem-wide mempolicy might be more suitable and easier to implement.

Reviewer noted that the current approach of requiring a mapping to get node-placement is defeating the point of enabling confidential, host-unmapped guest memory isolation and suggested exploring an alternative approach similar to HugeTLBfs.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng questioned whether lazy allocation is necessary, suggesting that pre-allocating memory using fallocate() before the guest accesses pages might be a viable alternative.
reviews.raw_body:
We have a similar problem where we wanted only guest memory to be
charged a certain memcg. Currently guest_memfd memory is charge to
mm->owner, which is the thread's parent, so doing the fallocate() in a
thread wasn't good enough. The workaround was to have the fallocate()
done in a separate process (fork) and have the child process's memcg be
set to the desired memcg.

This workaround is kind of awkward, but could it technically work for
NUMA allocations?

---

Off the top of my head the policy would be saved at gi->policy, where
it's stored for mbind() now. fd+offset is just another way of
referencing the offsets to set the policy.

---

Great! :) Cya!

Along the above lines, for HugeTLBfs we'd do something similar, and the
mount's fd would also indicate the HugeTLB page size.

Relating to memcg above, this doesn't really help though, since tmpfs
doesn't offer a way to configure memcgs.

---

Is lazy allocation a requirement for you? (as opposed to fallocate()-ing
before the guest touches pages)

reviews.author: Gregory Price (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged that the proposed work-around is clunky and not a good user behavior expectation, but did not agree to fix it; also pointed out that the issue of ineligible memory remains unresolved.

Author acknowledged that the scope of the patch is not suitable for all system memory, but expressed uncertainty about how to handle random file descriptors and reclaimed inodes.

Author acknowledged Ackerley Tng's concern about the scope of the patch and the need for per-file memory policies, but expressed skepticism about implementing such a feature, suggesting it might be over-engineering.

Author acknowledged that future overcommit handling is a consideration and decided to include it in the initial implementation.
sentiment_signals: decided to address it from the start
reviews.raw_body:
That is a very clunky work-around, I'm not sure it's good to formalize
that kind of design as an expected user behavior.

Whatever the case, the issue of ineligible memory isn't resolved by
this.  A node may be 100% ZONE_MOVABLE, and later entirely unmapped -
literally no eligible memory for kernel allocations for the task itself.

---

It makes sense for anon use cases like this, but for some random file
where fbind() means "put unmapped page cache on node X" the story is
less clear.

---

The only thing i've considered is something like GPU wanting a file
faulted directly onto its node - but that's a mapped region, and that's
handled by existing semantics.

---

Yes, because eventually some kind of overcommit will be desired. May as
well build it in from the start.

Looking forward to LPC :]

~Gregory

2026-09-09.patch_summary: This patch series aims to bind guest memory in KVM to a specific NUMA node, rather than all system memory for a process. The goal is to enable confidential and isolated virtual machines that are quarantined to a particular device without affecting the host's memory. To achieve this, the patch reduces the scope of the problem by focusing on the narrowest use-case, which is binding guest memory to a NUMA node. This approach is considered more feasible than other alternatives, such as implementing per-file memory policies or using fbind().
